The electron cloud of a π bond is located above and below the plane of the atoms.
Rotation around a π bond is restricted.
π bonds are centers of high electron density and are often the site of chemical reactions in unsaturated compounds.

source_text: The Lewis structure or dot structure, dash structure, condensed structure and bond line structural formulas are some of the specific types... For further simplification, organic chemists use another way of representing the structures, in which only lines are used. In this bond-line structural representation...
features: Complete Structural Formula (Dash Formula): Shows all atoms and bonds in a molecule.
Condensed Structural Formula: Omits some or all of the covalent bonds and indicates identical groups by a subscript (e.g., CH₃CH₂CH₃).

Bond-line Structural Formula: Carbon and hydrogen atoms are not shown. Carbon-carbon bonds are represented by lines in a zig-zag fashion. Vertices and terminals represent carbon atoms, which are assumed to be bonded to the appropriate number of hydrogens.

source_text: The functional group is an atom or a group of atoms joined to the carbon chain which is responsible for the characteristic chemical properties of the organic compounds. ... A group or a series of organic compounds each containing a characteristic functional group forms a homologous series...
features: A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms within a molecule that determines its characteristic chemical properties.
Examples of functional groups include hydroxyl (-OH), aldehyde (-CHO), carboxylic acid (-COOH), and amino (-NH₂).
A homologous series is a series of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties in which successive members differ by a -CH₂ group.

source_text: Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures (manners in which atoms are linked) are classified as structural isomers... The compounds that have the same constitution and sequence of covalent bonds but differ in relative positions of their atoms or groups in space are called stereoisomers.
features: Isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different properties.

Structural Isomerism: Isomers have different connectivity of atoms. Types include: Chain Isomerism (different carbon skeleton), Position Isomerism (different position of functional group/substituent), Functional Group Isomerism (different functional groups), and Metamerism (different alkyl groups on either side of a functional group).
Stereoisomerism: Isomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements of atoms. Types include Geometrical (cis-trans) Isomerism and Optical Isomerism.

source_text: A covalent bond can get cleaved either by : (i) heterolytic cleavage, or by (ii) homolytic cleavage. In heterolytic cleavage, the bond breaks in such a fashion that the shared pair of electrons remains with one of the fragments... In homolytic cleavage, one of the electrons of the shared pair in a covalent bond goes with each of the bonded atoms.
topic: Fission of Covalent Bonds and Reactive Intermediates
features: Heterolytic Cleavage: Unequal breaking of a covalent bond, where one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming a cation and an anion.
Carbocation: A positively charged species with a carbon atom having a sextet of electrons (e.g., CH₃⁺). Stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
Carbanion: A negatively charged species with a carbon atom having a lone pair of electrons (e.g., CH₃⁻).
Homolytic Cleavage: Equal breaking of a covalent bond, where each atom takes one bonding electron, forming free radicals.
Free Radical: A neutral species with an unpaired electron. Stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

source_text: A reagent that brings an electron pair to the reactive site is called a nucleophile (Nu:)... A reagent that takes away an electron pair from reactive site is called electrophile (E+)...
features: Nucleophile ('nucleus seeking'): An electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to form a new bond. Can be negatively charged (e.g., OH⁻, CN⁻) or neutral with lone pairs (e.g., H₂O, NH₃).

Electrophile ('electron seeking'): An electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair to form a new bond. Can be positively charged (e.g., H⁺, NO₂⁺, carbocations) or neutral with an electron-deficient center (e.g., BF₃, AlCl₃).

source_text: The electron displacement in an organic molecule may take place either in the ground state... or in the presence of an appropriate attacking reagent. ... Inductive effect and resonance effects are examples of this type of electron displacements [permanent]. Temporary electron displacement effects... is called electromeric effect...
features: Inductive Effect (I-effect): Permanent polarization of a sigma (σ) bond due to the electronegativity difference between bonded atoms. Electron-withdrawing groups (-I effect, e.g., -NO₂, -CN, halogens) and electron-donating groups (+I effect, e.g., alkyl groups).

Resonance (Mesomeric) Effect (R/M-effect): Permanent delocalization of pi (π) electrons in conjugated systems. Involves electron-donating (+R effect, e.g., -OH, -NH₂) and electron-withdrawing groups (-R effect, e.g., -NO₂, -CHO).
Electromeric Effect (E-effect): A temporary effect involving the complete transfer of a shared pair of π-electrons to one of the atoms in the presence of an attacking reagent.

Hyperconjugation: Delocalization of σ-electrons of a C-H bond of an alkyl group attached to an atom with an unshared p-orbital. Also known as 'no-bond resonance'. It is used to explain the stability of carbocations, alkenes, and free radicals.

source_text: Alkanes are saturated open chain hydrocarbons containing carbon - carbon single bonds. ... These hydrocarbons are inert under normal conditions as they do not react with acids, bases and other reagents. Hence, they were earlier known as paraffins...
features: General formula: CnH2n+2.
All carbon atoms are sp³ hybridized, resulting in a tetrahedral geometry around each carbon.
They are saturated hydrocarbons containing only C-C and C-H single (sigma) bonds.
Due to their non-polar nature and strong sigma bonds, they are relatively unreactive.
They primarily undergo free-radical substitution reactions (e.g., halogenation) and combustion.
Exhibit conformational isomerism (staggered and eclipsed forms) due to free rotation around C-C single bonds.

source_text: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one double bond... The presence of weaker π-bond makes alkenes unstable molecules in comparison to alkanes and thus, alkenes can be changed into single bond compounds by combining with the electrophilic reagents.
features: General formula: CnH2n.
Contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond (one σ bond, one π bond).
The doubly bonded carbon atoms are sp² hybridized, resulting in a trigonal planar geometry.
The π bond acts as a source of loosely held electrons, making alkenes reactive towards electrophiles.
The characteristic reaction of alkenes is electrophilic addition.
They exhibit geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism due to restricted rotation about the C=C bond.

source_text: Markovnikov rule. The rule states that negative part of the addendum (adding molecule) gets attached to that carbon atom which possesses lesser number of hydrogen atoms. ... Anti Markovnikov addition or peroxide effect or Kharash effect. In the presence of peroxide, addition of HBr to unsymmetrical alkenes like propene takes place contrary to the Markovnikov rule.
topic: Reactions of Alkenes: Markovnikov and Anti-Markovnikov Rules
features: Markovnikov's Rule: During the electrophilic addition of an unsymmetrical reagent (like HX) to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part of the reagent adds to the carbon atom of the double bond which has fewer hydrogen atoms. The mechanism involves the formation of a more stable carbocation intermediate.

Anti-Markovnikov's Rule (Peroxide Effect or Kharash Effect): In the presence of a peroxide, the addition of HBr (only HBr) to an unsymmetrical alkene occurs contrary to Markovnikov's rule. The mechanism involves a free radical pathway, forming a more stable free radical intermediate.

source_text: Alkynes are also unsaturated hydrocarbons. They contain at least one triple bond between two carbon atoms. ... hydrogen atoms of ethyne attached to triply bonded carbon atom are acidic in nature.
features: General formula: CnH2n-2.
Contain at least one carbon-carbon triple bond (one σ bond, two π bonds).
The triply bonded carbon atoms are sp hybridized, resulting in a linear geometry.
Terminal alkynes (with a hydrogen attached to a triply bonded carbon) are weakly acidic. This is due to the high s-character (50%) of the sp hybrid orbital, which makes the C-H bond more polar.
Like alkenes, they undergo addition reactions (e.g., hydrogenation, halogenation, addition of HX).

source_text: Benzene and benzenoid compounds show aromatic character. Aromaticity, the property of being aromatic is possessed by compounds having specific electronic structure characterised by Hückel (4n+2)π electron rule. ... Arenes are characterised by electrophilic substitution reactions.
features: Aromatic hydrocarbons are cyclic compounds containing one or more benzene rings or having properties similar to benzene.
Benzene (C₆H₆) is a planar, cyclic molecule with all six carbon atoms being sp² hybridized.
It exhibits resonance, with the π electrons delocalized over the entire ring, leading to unusual stability.
Hückel's Rule for Aromaticity: A compound is aromatic if it is planar, cyclic, has a continuous ring of p-orbitals, and contains (4n+2) π electrons (where n = 0, 1, 2, ...).
The characteristic reaction of aromatic compounds is electrophilic substitution (e.g., nitration, halogenation, sulfonation, Friedel-Crafts reactions), not addition.

source_text: Ortho and para directing groups: The groups which direct the incoming group to ortho and para positions are called ortho and para directing groups... Meta directing group: The groups which direct the incoming group to meta position are called meta directing groups.
topic: Directive Influence of Substituents in Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
features: Substituents already present on a benzene ring determine the position of the next incoming electrophile.

Activating Groups (Ortho, Para-directing): These groups donate electron density to the ring, making it more reactive towards electrophiles. They direct the incoming group to the ortho and para positions. Examples: -OH, -NH₂, -OR, -CH₃.

Deactivating Groups (Meta-directing): These groups withdraw electron density from the ring, making it less reactive. They direct the incoming group to the meta position. Examples: -NO₂, -CN, -CHO, -COOH, -SO₃H.
Halogens (Ortho, Para-directing Deactivators): Halogens are an exception. They are deactivating due to their strong -I effect but are ortho, para-directing due to their +R (resonance) effect.

source_text: Intermolecular forces are the forces of attraction and repulsion between interacting particles (atoms and molecules)... Attractive intermolecular forces are known as van der Waals forces... these forces include: (1) Dispersion Forces or London Forces (2) Dipole-Dipole Forces (3) Dipole-Induced Dipole Forces. A particularly strong type of dipole-dipole interaction is the hydrogen bond.
features: Intermolecular forces are the attractive or repulsive forces between neighboring entities (atoms, molecules, or ions).
van der Waals forces are a subset of intermolecular forces and include London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, and dipole-induced dipole forces.
London Dispersion Forces: Exist in all atoms and molecules. They arise from temporary, instantaneous dipoles and are the only forces present in nonpolar molecules.
Dipole-Dipole Forces: Act between polar molecules that have permanent dipoles.
Dipole-Induced Dipole Forces: Arise when a polar molecule induces a temporary dipole in a nonpolar molecule.
Hydrogen Bond: A strong type of dipole-dipole interaction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and another nearby electronegative atom.

source_text: Boyle’s Law: At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount (i.e., number of moles n) of gas varies inversely with its volume. ... Charles’ Law: pressure remaining constant, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. ... Gay Lussac’s Law: At constant volume, pressure of a fixed amount of a gas varies directly with the temperature. ... Avogadro Law: It states that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.
features: Boyle's Law: At constant temperature, P ∝ 1/V or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Charles's Law: At constant pressure, V ∝ T (in Kelvin) or V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
Gay-Lussac's Law: At constant volume, P ∝ T (in Kelvin) or P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂.
Avogadro's Law: At constant temperature and pressure, V ∝ n (number of moles) or V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂.

source_text: These three laws can be combined together in a single equation which is known as ideal gas equation. pV = nRT. ... Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures: It states that the total pressure exerted by the mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of individual gases...
topic: Ideal Gas Equation and Dalton's Law
features: The Ideal Gas Equation combines Boyle's Law, Charles's Law, and Avogadro's Law into a single relationship: pV = nRT.
In the equation, p is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, T is the absolute temperature, and R is the universal gas constant (approx. 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ or 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
An ideal gas is a hypothetical gas that perfectly follows this equation under all conditions.
Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases is the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases (P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...).
The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is related to the total pressure by the equation Pᵢ = xᵢ * P_total, where xᵢ is the mole fraction of gas i.

source_text: The deviation from ideal behaviour can be measured in terms of compressibility factor Z, which is the ratio of product pV and nRT. Z = pV/nRT... The van der Waals equation is: (p + an²/V²)(V-nb) = nRT
topic: Real Gases and Deviation from Ideal Behavior
features: Real gases deviate from ideal behavior, especially at high pressure and low temperature.
This deviation is due to two incorrect assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory: (1) the volume of gas molecules is negligible, and (2) there are no intermolecular forces of attraction.
Compressibility factor (Z = pV/nRT) is used to quantify the deviation. For an ideal gas, Z=1. For real gases, Z can be greater or less than 1.
The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law for real gases: For real gases, Z can be greater or less than 1.
The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law for real gases:  (p + a(n/V)²)(V - nb) = nRT.

source_text: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, 1H, deuterium, 2H or D and tritium, 3H or T. ... Because of this similarity in electronic configuration, hydrogen has many properties in common with alkali metals. Also like halogens, it is short by one electron to the corresponding noble gas configuration...
features: Hydrogen has a unique position in the periodic table, showing resemblances to both alkali metals (Group 1) and halogens (Group 17).
It has three isotopes: Protium (¹H, most common), Deuterium (²H or D, heavy hydrogen), and Tritium (³H or T, radioactive).
Dihydrogen (H₂) can be prepared by reacting active metals with acids, or by the electrolysis of water.
It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, combustible gas, which is the lightest substance known.
Chemically, it acts as a good reducing agent and reacts with halogens, dioxygen, dinitrogen, and metals to form hydrides.

source_text: The hardness of water is due to the presence of calcium and magnesium salts (bicarbonates, chlorides and sulphates) in it. It does not give lather with soap. Water free from soluble salts of calcium and magnesium is called soft water. ... Temporary hardness is due to the presence of magnesium and calcium hydrogencarbonates... Permanent hardness is on account of the presence of soluble salts of magnesium and calcium in the form of chlorides and sulphates in water.
features: Hard water contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium, which prevents soap from lathering.
Soft water is free from these soluble salts.
Temporary Hardness: Caused by the presence of magnesium and calcium hydrogencarbonates [Mg(HCO₃)₂ and Ca(HCO₃)₂]. It can be removed by boiling or by Clark's method (adding lime).
Permanent Hardness: Caused by the presence of chlorides and sulfates of calcium and magnesium. It cannot be removed by boiling.
Methods to remove permanent hardness include treatment with washing soda (sodium carbonate), Calgon's method, ion-exchange method, and synthetic resins method.

source_text: The s-block elements of the Periodic Table are those in which the last electron enters the outermost s-orbital. As the s-orbital can accommodate only two electrons, two groups (1 & 2) belong to the s-block of the Periodic Table. Group 1 of the Periodic Table consists of the elements: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium. They are collectively known as the alkali metals. ... Group 2 includes beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium. These elements with the exception of beryllium are commonly known as the alkaline earth metals.
features: s-Block elements have their last electron entering the outermost s-orbital.
Group 1 elements are called Alkali Metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) and have an outer electronic configuration of ns¹.
Group 2 elements are called Alkaline Earth Metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) and have an outer electronic configuration of ns².
Alkali metals are highly reactive, soft, low-density metals with low ionization enthalpies.
Alkaline earth metals are also reactive (though less than alkali metals), harder, and denser than alkali metals.

source_text: The anomalous behaviour of lithium is due to the : (i) exceptionally small size of its atom and ion, and (ii) high polarising power (i.e., charge/ radius ratio). ... The similarity between lithium and magnesium is particularly striking and arises because of their similar sizes: atomic radii, Li = 152 pm, Mg = 160 pm; ionic radii : Li+ = 76 pm, Mg2+ = 72 pm. This is known as a diagonal relationship.
topic: Anomalous Properties of Lithium and Beryllium, and Diagonal Relationships
features: The first element of each s-block group (Lithium and Beryllium) shows anomalous behavior due to its exceptionally small size, high ionization enthalpy, and high polarizing power.

Lithium shows a diagonal relationship with Magnesium (Mg). Similarities include forming nitrides, having hard carbonates and hydroxides that decompose on heating, and having covalent character in their halides.

Beryllium shows a diagonal relationship with Aluminium (Al). Similarities include resistance to acid attack due to a protective oxide layer, formation of covalent halides, and amphoteric nature of their oxides and hydroxides.

source_text: The p-Block Elements comprise those belonging to Group 13 to 18... Their valence shell electronic configuration is ns²np¹⁻⁶... The reluctance of ns² electrons of the valence shell to participate in bond formation is termed as the inert pair effect.
topic: Introduction to p-Block Elements and Inert Pair Effect
features: p-Block elements are those where the last electron enters the p-orbital of the outermost shell.
They comprise groups 13 to 18 of the periodic table.
The general outer electronic configuration is ns²np¹⁻⁶.
The p-block is the only block that contains metals, nonmetals, and metalloids.

Inert Pair Effect: The tendency of the two electrons in the outermost s-orbital to remain unshared in compounds of post-transition metals. This effect increases down a group and explains why heavier elements of groups 13, 14, and 15 exhibit oxidation states that are two less than the group oxidation state (e.g., Tl⁺ is more stable than Tl³⁺, Pb²⁺ is more stable than Pb⁴⁺).

source_text: Group 13 Elements: The Boron Family... Boron is a typical non-metal, aluminium is a metal but shows many chemical similarities to boron, and gallium, indium and thallium are almost exclusively metallic in character. ... Boron is unable to form BF₆³⁻ ion.
features: The elements are Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), Gallium (Ga), Indium (In), and Thallium (Tl).
The general outer electronic configuration is ns²np¹.
Boron is a non-metal/metalloid, while the rest are metals.
The common oxidation state is +3, but due to the inert pair effect, +1 oxidation state becomes progressively more stable down the group (especially for Tl).
Boron shows anomalous behavior due to its small size, high ionization enthalpy, and absence of d-orbitals. It cannot expand its octet.
Boron and Aluminium compounds often act as Lewis acids due to their incomplete octet (e.g., BF₃, AlCl₃).

source_text: Carbon exhibits the property of catenation to the maximum extent... Carbon also forms pπ–pπ multiple bonds to itself and to other small atoms... Diamond... Graphite... Fullerenes...
topic: Group 14 Elements: The Carbon Family and Allotropes of Carbon
features: The elements are Carbon (C), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Tin (Sn), and Lead (Pb).
The general outer electronic configuration is ns²np².
Carbon is a non-metal; Silicon and Germanium are metalloids; Tin and Lead are metals.
The common oxidation states are +4 and +2. The stability of the +2 state increases down the group due to the inert pair effect.
Carbon shows unique properties of catenation (self-linking to form long chains and rings) and formation of pπ–pπ multiple bonds.

Allotropes of Carbon: Diamond (sp³ hybridized, tetrahedral, hardest substance), Graphite (sp² hybridized, layered structure, soft and a good conductor of electricity), and Fullerenes (sp² hybridized, cage-like molecules, e.g., C₆₀ Buckminsterfullerene).

source_text: Environmental chemistry deals with the study of the origin, transport, reactions, effects and fates of chemical species in the environment. ... Atmospheric pollution: The atmosphere... is divided into four regions... Troposphere... Stratosphere... Mesosphere... Thermosphere.
topic: Introduction to Environmental Chemistry and Atmospheric Pollution
features: Environmental Chemistry is the scientific study of chemical and biochemical phenomena that occur in natural places.
Atmospheric Pollution is the presence of undesirable materials in the air in concentrations large enough to produce harmful effects.

Tropospheric Pollution: Occurs in the lowest region of the atmosphere. Gaseous pollutants include oxides of sulphur (SOx), nitrogen (NOx), carbon (CO, CO₂), and hydrocarbons. Particulate pollutants include dust, mist, fumes, and smoke.
Stratospheric Pollution: The main issue is the depletion of the ozone layer, primarily caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

source_text: The increase in the global temperature is called global warming... Acid rain is a byproduct of a variety of human activities that emit the oxides of sulphur and nitrogen in the atmosphere... Photochemical smog is a complex mixture of compounds formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds (hydrocarbons) react to sunlight.
features: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming: The trapping of solar energy by greenhouse gases (like CO₂, CH₄, O₃, CFCs) leads to the heating up of the Earth's atmosphere.

Acid Rain: Oxides of nitrogen and sulfur react with atmospheric water to form nitric acid and sulfuric acid, which fall to the earth as acid rain (pH < 5.6). It damages buildings, forests, and aquatic life.

Photochemical Smog: A type of smog produced when ultraviolet light from the sun reacts with nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere. It is characterized by high concentrations of ozone at ground level and is a powerful respiratory irritant.

Ozone Layer Depletion: CFCs release chlorine free radicals in the stratosphere, which catalytically destroy ozone molecules, leading to the formation of the 'ozone hole' and allowing harmful UV radiation to reach the Earth's surface.

source_text: Pollution of water originates from human activities. ... Pathogens... Organic wastes... Chemical pollutants... The amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down the organic matter present in a certain volume of a sample of water, is called Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)... The process in which nutrient enriched water bodies support a dense plant population... is known as Eutrophication.
features: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies, usually as a result of human activities.
Major pollutants include pathogens (disease-causing bacteria), organic wastes (from sewage), and chemical pollutants (heavy metals, fertilizers, pesticides).

Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD): A measure of the amount of dissolved oxygen required by aerobic biological organisms to break down organic material present in a given water sample. High BOD indicates a high level of organic pollution.

Eutrophication: The enrichment of water bodies with nutrients (like nitrates and phosphates), which leads to excessive growth of algae (algal bloom). This depletes dissolved oxygen, killing aquatic life.

source_text: Green chemistry is a way of thinking and is about utilising the existing knowledge and principles of chemistry and other sciences to reduce the adverse impact on environment. Green chemistry is a production process that would bring about minimum pollution or deterioration to the environment.
features: Green Chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances.
It aims to make chemistry more environmentally friendly and sustainable.
Key principles include waste prevention, maximizing atom economy, using less hazardous chemical syntheses, and designing for energy efficiency.
Examples include using H₂O₂ as a cleaner oxidizing agent instead of traditional reagents and using supercritical CO₂ as a green solvent.

source_text: Elements, their Atomic Number and Molar Mass. ... The value given in parenthesis is the molar mass of the isotope of largest known half-life.
topic: Properties of Elements from Appendix II
features: Appendix II provides a comprehensive list of elements with their chemical symbol, atomic number (Z), and molar mass (in g/mol ).
The atomic number represents the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.
The molar mass is the mass of one mole of an element's atoms.
For radioactive elements, the molar mass provided in parentheses corresponds to the mass number of the most stable or common long-lived isotope.

source_text: A. Specific and Molar Heat Capacities for Some Substances at 298 K and one Atmospheric Pressure. Substance Specific Heat Capacity (J/g) Molar Heat Capacity (J/mol). ... B. Molar Heat Capacities for Some Gases (J/mol). Gas Cp Cv Cp - Cv Cp / Cv
features: Specific Heat Capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 Kelvin (or 1°C). Units are J/g or J g⁻¹K⁻¹.
Molar Heat Capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 mole of a substance by 1 Kelvin (or 1°C). Units are J/mol or J mol⁻¹K⁻¹.
For gases, heat capacity is measured at constant pressure (Cp) and constant volume (Cv).
The ratio of molar heat capacities (Cp/Cv) is known as the heat capacity ratio (gamma, γ).
For monatomic gases, Cp/Cv is approximately 1.66.
For diatomic gases, Cp/Cv is approximately 1.40.

source_text: Physical Constants. Avogadro constant NA 6.022 × 10²³ particles/mol. Boltzmann constant k 1.3807 × 10⁻²³ J/K. Planck constant h 6.6262 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Speed of light c 2.9979 × 10⁸ m/s.
features: Avogadro Constant (NA): The number of elementary entities per mole, approximately 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Boltzmann Constant (k): A proportionality factor that relates the average relative kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas, approximately 1.3807 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
Planck Constant (h): A fundamental constant in quantum mechanics that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency, approximately 6.6262 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
Speed of Light in vacuum (c): The speed at which all electromagnetic radiation travels in a vacuum, approximately 2.9979 × 10⁸ m/s.
Gas Constant (R): A physical constant which is featured in many equations in the physical sciences, such as the ideal gas law. R ≈ 8.3145 J/(mol·K).

source_text: Some Useful Conversion Factors. 1 pound = 453.59 grams. 1 litre = 1.056 quarts. 1 inch = 2.54 centimetres (exactly). 1 atmosphere = 760 millimetres of mercury = 1.013 × 10⁵ pascals. 1 thermochemical calorie = 4.184 joules.
features: Mass: 1 pound = 453.59 g; 1 kilogram = 2.205 pounds.
Length: 1 inch = 2.54 cm (exact); 1 mile = 1.609 km.
Volume: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1 dm³.
Pressure: 1 atmosphere (atm) = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 1.01325 × 10⁵ Pa = 1.01325 bar.
Energy: 1 calorie (cal) = 4.184 Joules (J); 1 electron volt (eV) = 1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Temperature: K = °C + 273.15

source_text: Thermodynamic Data at 298 K. Substance Enthalpy of formation, ΔfH°/ (kJ mol⁻¹) Gibbs Energy of formation, ΔfG°/ (kJ mol⁻¹) Entropy, S°/(J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
features: Standard Enthalpy of Formation (ΔfH°): The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states (usually at 298 K and 1 bar). The ΔfH° of an element in its most stable form is zero.
Standard Gibbs Free Energy of Formation (ΔfG°): The change in Gibbs free energy that accompanies the formation of one mole of a substance from its component elements in their standard states.
Standard Entropy (S°): The entropy content of one mole of a substance under standard state conditions. Unlike enthalpy and Gibbs energy of formation, the standard entropy of an element is not zero.
These values can be used to calculate the standard enthalpy (ΔrH°), entropy (ΔrS°), and Gibbs free energy (ΔrG°) for a chemical reaction.

source_text: Standard potentials at 298 K in electrochemical order. Reduction half-reaction E°/V. F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻, +2.87. ... 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, 0.00 by definition. ... Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li, -3.05.
features: Standard Electrode Potential (E°) is the measure of the tendency of a chemical species to be reduced, and is measured at standard conditions (298 K, 1 M concentration, 1 bar pressure).
Potentials are measured relative to the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), which is assigned a potential of 0.00 V.
A more positive E° value indicates a greater tendency for the species to be reduced (i.e., it is a stronger oxidizing agent).
A more negative E° value indicates a lesser tendency for the species to be reduced (i.e., its conjugate oxidized form is a stronger reducing agent).
Fluorine (F₂) has the highest standard reduction potential (+2.87 V), making it the strongest oxidizing agent.
Lithium (Li) has the most negative standard reduction potential (-3.05 V), making it the strongest reducing agent.

source_text: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures of two or more than two components. By homogenous mixture we mean that its composition and properties are uniform throughout the mixture. Generally, the component that is present in the largest quantity is known as solvent. Solvent determines the physical state in which solution exists. One or more components present in the solution other than solvent are called solutes.
features: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components.
Homogeneous means the composition and properties are uniform.
The component in the largest quantity is the solvent.
Components other than the solvent are called solutes.

source_text: Henry’s law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas present above the surface of liquid or solution. The most commonly used form of Henry’s law states that “the partial pressure of the gas in vapour phase (p) is proportional to the mole fraction of the gas (x) in the solution” and is expressed as: p = KH * x
features: The solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure.
The partial pressure (p) of a gas is proportional to its mole fraction (x) in the solution.
Formula: p = KH * x, where KH is Henry's law constant.
Higher the value of KH at a given pressure, the lower is the solubility of the gas.

source_text: Raoult’s law... states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component of the solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction present in solution. Thus, for component 1, p1 ∝ x1 and p1 = p1°x1, where p1° is the vapour pressure of pure component 1.
features: The partial vapour pressure of a component in a solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction.
Formula for a component: p₁ = p₁°x₁, where p₁° is the vapor pressure of the pure component.
This law applies to solutions containing volatile liquids.

source_text: All these properties depend on the number of solute particles irrespective of their nature relative to the total number of particles present in the solution. Such properties are called colligative properties. These are: (1) relative lowering of vapour pressure of the solvent (2) depression of freezing point of the solvent (3) elevation of boiling point of the solvent and (4) osmotic pressure of the solution.
features: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their identity.
The four colligative properties are: relative lowering of vapor pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure.

source_text: A galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. If an external opposite potential is applied... and increased slowly... Any further increase in the external potential again starts the reaction but in the opposite direction. It now functions as an electrolytic cell, a device for using electrical energy to carry non-spontaneous chemical reactions.
features: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy via a spontaneous redox reaction.
An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
The direction of cell operation can be reversed by applying an external potential greater than the cell potential.

source_text: Nernst showed that for the electrode reaction: Mn+(aq) + ne– → M(s), the electrode potential at any concentration measured with respect to standard hydrogen electrode can be represented by: E(M^(n+)/M) = E°(M^(n+)/M) - (RT/nF)ln(1/[M^(n+)])
features: The Nernst equation relates the electrode potential (E) at any concentration to the standard electrode potential (E°).
It accounts for the effect of ion concentration and temperature on electrode potential.
At 298 K, the equation simplifies to E = E° - (0.059/n)log(1/[M^(n+)]).

source_text: First Law: The amount of chemical reaction which occurs at any electrode during electrolysis by a current is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte. Second Law: The amounts of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity passing through the electrolytic solution are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.
features: First Law: The mass of substance reacted is proportional to the total electric charge passed (Q = It).
Second Law: For the same amount of electricity, the mass of different substances liberated is proportional to their equivalent weights.

source_text: The rate of a reaction can be defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product in unit time. rate law is the expression in which reaction rate is given in terms of molar concentration of reactants with each term raised to some power, which may or may not be same as the stoichiometric coefficient... The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the rate law expression is called the order of that chemical reaction.
topic: Rate, Rate Law, and Order of Reaction
features: Rate of reaction is the change in concentration over time.
Rate law expresses the reaction rate as a function of reactant concentrations.
The order of a reaction is the sum of the exponents in the rate law expression and must be determined experimentally.

source_text: The number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction, which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of a reaction. Order of a reaction is an experimental quantity. It can be zero and even a fraction but molecularity cannot be zero or a non integer.
features: Molecularity is the number of reacting species in an elementary (single-step) reaction.
Molecularity is a theoretical concept and must be a positive integer (1, 2, or 3).
Order is an experimental value and can be zero, fractional, or an integer, while molecularity cannot.

source_text: The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration. It is represented as t1/2. For a zero order reaction, t1/2 ∝ [R]₀. For a first order reaction, t1/2 is independent of [R]₀.
features: Half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for the reactant concentration to become half of its initial value.
For a zero-order reaction, half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration.
For a first-order reaction, half-life is constant and independent of the initial concentration.

source_text: transition metals are defined as metals which have incomplete d subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions. Zinc, cadmium and mercury of group 12 have full d10 configuration in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states and hence, are not regarded as transition metals.
features: Transition metals are elements with a partially filled d subshell in their neutral or ionic state.
Group 12 elements (Zn, Cd, Hg) are not considered transition metals because they have a full d¹⁰ configuration.

source_text: The overall decrease in atomic and ionic radii from lanthanum to lutetium (the lanthanoid contraction) is a unique feature... The net result of the lanthanoid contraction is that the second and the third d series exhibit similar radii (e.g., Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) and have very similar physical and chemical properties.
features: Lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoid elements with increasing atomic number.
It is caused by the poor shielding effect of 4f electrons.
A key consequence is the similarity in size and properties between the 4d and 5d transition series elements (e.g., Zr and Hf).

source_text: One of the notable features of a transition elements is the great variety of oxidation states these may show in their compounds... The variability of oxidation states, a characteristic of transition elements, arises out of incomplete filling of d orbitals in such a way that their oxidation states differ from each other by unity.
topic: Variable Oxidation States of Transition Metals
features: Transition metals exhibit a wide range of oxidation states.
This is due to the small energy difference between the (n-1)d and ns orbitals, allowing electrons from both to participate in bonding.
Oxidation states typically differ by one unit (e.g., Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺).

source_text: Werner in 1898, propounded his theory of coordination compounds. The main postulates are: 1. In coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages (valences)-primary and secondary. 2. The primary valences are normally ionisable... 3. The secondary valences are non ionisable... The secondary valence is equal to the coordination number.
features: Metals in coordination compounds exhibit two types of valences: primary and secondary.
Primary valence corresponds to the oxidation state and is ionizable.
Secondary valence corresponds to the coordination number, is non-ionizable, and determines the geometry of the complex.

source_text: Isomers are two or more compounds that have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms. Two principal types of isomerism are known among coordination compounds. Each of which can be further subdivided. (a) Stereoisomerism (Geometrical and Optical). (b) Structural isomerism (Linkage, Coordination, Ionisation and Solvate).
features: Isomers have the same chemical formula but different arrangements of atoms.
Stereoisomerism includes geometrical (cis-trans, fac-mer) and optical isomers.
Structural isomerism includes linkage, coordination, ionization, and solvate isomers.

source_text: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal-ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand. This splitting of the degenerate levels due to the presence of ligands in a definite geometry is termed as crystal field splitting.
features: CFT treats the metal-ligand bond as purely electrostatic (ionic).
It explains the splitting of the degenerate d-orbitals of the metal ion in the presence of the electric field of the ligands.
The pattern of splitting (e.g., t₂g and eg in octahedral fields) depends on the geometry of the complex.

source_text: In alkyl halides, the halogen atom is bonded to an alkyl group (R). They form a homologous series represented by CnH2n+1X. In aryl halides, the halogen atom is directly bonded to the sp2-hybridised carbon atom of an aromatic ring.
features: In haloalkanes (alkyl halides), the halogen is attached to an sp³-hybridized carbon.
In haloarenes (aryl halides), the halogen is attached to an sp²-hybridized carbon of an aromatic ring.

source_text: Substitution nucleophilic bimolecular (SN2)... depicts a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction; the incoming nucleophile interacts with alkyl halide causing the carbon-halide bond to break and a new bond is formed... in a single step... Substitution nucleophilic unimolecular (SN1)... reaction occurs in two steps. In step I, the polarised C—Br bond undergoes slow cleavage to produce a carbocation and a bromide ion.
features: SN2 reactions are bimolecular and occur in a single step with inversion of configuration.
The order of reactivity for SN2 is Primary halide > Secondary halide > Tertiary halide.
SN1 reactions are unimolecular and occur in two steps via a carbocation intermediate, leading to racemization.
The order of reactivity for SN1 is Tertiary halide > Secondary halide > Primary halide.

source_text: Aryl halides are extremely less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions... due to resonance effect, the C—Cl bond acquires a partial double bond character... [and] difference in hybridisation of carbon atom in C—X bond (sp2 in aryl halide).
topic: Reactivity of Haloarenes in Nucleophilic Substitution
features: Aryl halides are much less reactive than alkyl halides towards nucleophilic substitution.
Reasons for low reactivity include the partial double-bond character of the C-X bond due to resonance.
The C-X bond involves an sp²-hybridized carbon, which is shorter and stronger than an sp³-hybridized C-X bond.

source_text: Alcohols and phenols may be classified as mono–, di–, tri- or polyhydric compounds depending on whether they contain one, two, three or many hydroxyl groups... Ethers are classified as simple or symmetrical, if the alkyl or aryl groups attached to the oxygen atom are the same, and mixed or unsymmetrical, if the two groups are different.
topic: Classification of Alcohols, Phenols, and Ethers
features: Alcohols and phenols are classified based on the number of -OH groups (mono-, di-, trihydric).
Alcohols are also classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°), or tertiary (3°).
Ethers are classified as symmetrical (simple) or unsymmetrical (mixed) based on the groups attached to the oxygen atom.

source_text: The acidic character of alcohols is due to the polar nature of O–H bond... The reaction of phenol with aqueous sodium hydroxide indicates that phenols are stronger acids than alcohols and water... The delocalisation of negative charge ... makes phenoxide ion more stable and favours the ionisation of phenol.
features: The acidity of alcohols is due to the polarity of the O-H bond.
Phenols are significantly more acidic than alcohols and water.
The higher acidity of phenols is due to the resonance stabilization of the phenoxide ion, which delocalizes the negative charge into the benzene ring.

source_text: Williamson synthesis. It is an important laboratory method for the preparation of symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers. In this method, an alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium alkoxide... The reaction involves SN2 attack of an alkoxide ion on primary alkyl halide. For secondary and tertiary alkyl halides, elimination is a competing reaction.
features: Williamson synthesis is a method to prepare both symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.
It involves an SN2 reaction between a sodium alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide.
If a secondary or tertiary alkyl halide is used, elimination becomes the major reaction pathway, producing an alkene instead of an ether.

source_text: The carbon-oxygen double bond is polarised due to higher electronegativity of oxygen relative to carbon. Hence, the carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic (Lewis acid), and carbonyl oxygen, a nucleophilic (Lewis base) centre... In carboxylic acids, the bonds to the carboxyl carbon lie in one plane... The carboxylic carbon is less electrophilic than carbonyl carbon because of the possible resonance structure.
topic: Structure of Carbonyl and Carboxyl Groups
features: The carbonyl group (>C=O) is polar, with an electrophilic carbon and a nucleophilic oxygen.
The geometry around the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar (sp² hybridized).
The carboxyl carbon in carboxylic acids is less electrophilic than in aldehydes or ketones due to resonance with the hydroxyl group.

source_text: Aldol condensation: Aldehydes and ketones having at least one α-hydrogen undergo a reaction in the presence of dilute alkali as catalyst... Cannizzaro reaction: Aldehydes which do not have an α-hydrogen atom, undergo self oxidation and reduction (disproportionation) reaction on heating with concentrated alkali.
features: Aldol condensation requires at least one α-hydrogen and uses a dilute base, forming β-hydroxy aldehydes/ketones.
The Cannizzaro reaction requires aldehydes with no α-hydrogen and uses a concentrated base.
The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation reaction, producing one molecule of alcohol and one molecule of carboxylic acid salt.

source_text: Effect of substituents on the acidity of carboxylic acids: Electron withdrawing groups increase the acidity of carboxylic acids by stabilising the conjugate base through delocalisation of the negative charge... Conversely, electron donating groups decrease the acidity by destabilising the conjugate base.
features: Carboxylic acids are acidic due to the resonance stabilization of the carboxylate anion conjugate base.
Electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) attached to the carboxylic acid increase its acidity by further stabilizing the conjugate base.
Electron-donating groups (EDGs) decrease acidity by destabilizing the conjugate base.

source_text: Amines are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°) and tertiary (3°) depending upon the number of hydrogen atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups in ammonia molecule. The order of basicity of amines in the gaseous phase follows the expected order: tertiary amine > secondary amine > primary amine > NH₃.
features: Amines are classified as primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH), and tertiary (R₃N).
Amines are basic due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.
In the gaseous phase, basicity increases with the number of alkyl groups due to the +I (inductive) effect: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.

source_text: pKb value of aniline is quite high. It is because in aniline or other arylamines, the –NH₂ group is attached directly to the benzene ring. It results in the unshared electron pair on nitrogen atom to be in conjugation with the benzene ring and thus making it less available for protonation.
features: Aromatic amines (like aniline) are significantly weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines.
This is because the lone pair on the nitrogen is delocalized into the benzene ring through resonance.
The delocalization makes the lone pair less available for protonation.

source_text: Aromatic amines react with nitrous acid at low temperatures (273-278 K) to form diazonium salts... The Cl⁻, Br⁻ and CN⁻ nucleophiles can easily be introduced in the benzene ring in the presence of Cu(I) ion. This reaction is called Sandmeyer reaction.
features: Primary aromatic amines form arenediazonium salts when treated with nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl) at low temperatures (0-5 °C).
This process is called diazotization.
The Sandmeyer reaction involves the replacement of the diazonium group with -Cl, -Br, or -CN using a Cu(I) salt.

source_text: The two cyclic hemiacetal forms of glucose differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C1, called anomeric carbon. Such isomers, i.e., α-form and β-form, are called anomers. The six membered cyclic structure of glucose is called pyranose structure.
topic: Cyclic Structure of Glucose and Anomers
features: Glucose exists in two cyclic hemiacetal forms: α-glucose and β-glucose.
These two isomers are called anomers.
Anomers differ in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at the anomeric carbon (C1).
The six-membered ring structure of glucose is called a pyranose ring.

source_text: Proteins are the polymers of α-amino acids and they are connected to each other by peptide bond... Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels, i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary... Primary structure of proteins... is the sequence of amino acids.
features: Proteins are polymers of α-amino acids linked by peptide bonds.
Primary structure refers to the specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.
Secondary structure refers to the local folding of the polypeptide chain (e.g., α-helix and β-pleated sheet).
Tertiary structure is the overall 3D shape of a single polypeptide chain.
Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits.

source_text: Nucleic acids are... of two types, the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA)... DNA contains four bases viz. adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). RNA... the fourth one is uracil (U)... The structure of DNA is a double strand whereas RNA is a single strand molecule.
features: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides.
The two main types are DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid).
DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose and the bases A, G, C, T.
RNA contains the sugar ribose and the bases A, G, C, U.
DNA has a double helix structure, while RNA is typically single-stranded.

subject: Chemistry
question: The ratio of the wavelengths of the light absorbed by a Hydrogen atom when it undergoes n = 2 → n = 3 and n = 4 → n = 6 transitions, respectively, is
brief_explanation: Using the Rydberg formula, 1/λ = R(1/n₁² - 1/n₂²). For the first transition (n=2 to n=3), 1/λ₁ = R(1/2² - 1/3²) = R(5/36). For the second transition (n=4 to n=6), 1/λ₂ = R(1/4² - 1/6²) = R(5/144). The ratio of the wavelengths λ₁/λ₂ is equal to (1/λ₂)/(1/λ₁) = (5R/144) / (5R/36) = 36/144 = 1/4.

question:
Which of the following statements are true?
A. Unlike Ga that has a very high melting point, Cs has a very low melting point.
B. On Pauling scale, the electronegativity values of N and Cl are not the same.
C. Ar, K⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺ and S²⁻ are all isoelectronic species.
D. The correct order of the first ionization enthalpies of Na, Mg, Al, and Si is Si > Al > Mg > Na.
E. The atomic radius of Cs is greater than that of Li and Rb.

Statement C is true (all have 18 electrons). Statement D is false (correct order is Si > Mg > Al > Na). Statement E is true (atomic radius increases down a group). Therefore, only statements C and E are definitively true.

question: Energy and radius of first Bohr orbit of He⁺ and Li²⁺ are [Given RH = 2.18×10⁻¹⁸ J, a₀ = 52.9 pm]

options.1: Eₙ(Li²⁺)=-19.62×10⁻¹⁸ J; rₙ(Li²⁺)=17.6 pm and Eₙ(He⁺)=-8.72×10⁻¹⁸ J; rₙ(He⁺)=26.4 pm
options.2: Eₙ(Li²⁺)=-8.72×10⁻¹⁸ J; rₙ(Li²⁺)=26.4 pm and Eₙ(He⁺)=-19.62×10⁻¹⁸ J; rₙ(He⁺)=17.6 pm
options.3: Values are given with exponent -16 J

For Li²⁺ (Z=3): E₁ = -Rₕ(3²/1²) = -9Rₕ = -19.62×10⁻¹⁸ J; r₁ = a₀(1²/3) = 17.6 pm. Option (1) matches these calculated values.

question: Which of the following are paramagnetic? A. [NiCl₄]²⁻ B. Ni(CO)₄ C. [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ D. [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ E. Ni(PPh₃)₄

D: [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (Ni²⁺, d⁸, weak field octahedral) has 2 unpaired electrons. B and E are Ni(0), d¹⁰, diamagnetic. C: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ (Ni²⁺, d⁸, strong field square planar) is diamagnetic. Thus, only A and D are paramagnetic.

question: If the half-life (t₁/₂) for a first order reaction is 1 minute, then the time required for 99.9% completion of the reaction is closest to:
brief_explanation: For a first-order reaction, the time required for 99.9% completion is approximately 10 times the half-life (t₉₉.₉ ≈ 10 × t₁/₂). Given t₁/₂ = 1 minute, the time for 99.9% completion will be approximately 10 × 1 = 10 minutes.

question: The correct order of the wavelength of light absorbed by the following complexes is, A. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ B. [Co(CN)₆]³⁻ C. [Cu(H₂O)₄]²⁺ D. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺
brief_explanation: The wavelength of light absorbed (λ) is inversely proportional to the crystal field splitting energy (Δ₀). The order of Δ₀ is determined by the spectrochemical series of ligands and the charge on the metal ion. Ligand strength: CN⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O. Metal ion effect: Co³⁺ > Ti³⁺ > Cu²⁺. Combining these, the Δ₀ order is B > A > D > C. Therefore, the wavelength order is the reverse: B < A < D < C.

question: Which one of the following compounds can exist as cis-trans isomers?
brief_explanation: Cis-trans (geometric) isomerism is possible in compounds with restricted rotation (like a ring or double bond) where each carbon involved in the restricted rotation has two different groups attached. In 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, both C-1 and C-2 have a methyl group and a hydrogen atom, allowing for cis and trans arrangements across the plane of the ring.

question: Phosphoric acid ionizes in three steps with their ionization constant values Kₐ₁, Kₐ₂, and Kₐ₃, respectively, while K is the overall ionization constant. Which of the following statements are true?
brief_explanation: Statement A is true, as the overall equilibrium constant is the product of stepwise constants (K = Kₐ₁·Kₐ₂·Kₐ₃), so their logs add up. Statement B is true because acidity decreases as protons are removed. Statement C is true as it's progressively harder to remove a proton from a more negatively charged species. Statement D is an incorrect mathematical relationship. Thus, A, B, and C are true.

question: If the molar conductivity (Λₘ) of a 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of a monobasic weak acid is 90 S cm² mol⁻¹, its extent (degree) of dissociation will be [Assume Λ°(H⁺) = 349.6 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°(A⁻) = 50.4 S cm² mol⁻¹]

Statement II: On the basis of molecular mass, $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is expected to have lower boiling point than the other members of the group but due to the presence of extensive $\mathrm{H}$-bonding in $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$, it has higher boiling point.

options.4: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

question: For the reaction $2 \mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{B}+\mathrm{C}$, $K_c=4 \times 10^{-3}$. At a given time, the composition of reaction mixture is: $[\mathrm{A}]=[\mathrm{B}]=[\mathrm{C}]=2 \times 10^{-2}~\mathrm{M}$. Then which of the following is correct?

options.2: Reaction has gone to completion in forward direction.

Since $\mathrm{Q}_c$ (1) $>$ $\mathrm{K}_c$ ($4 \times 10^{-3}$), the reaction will proceed in the backward direction to reach equilibrium.

brief_explanation: $\mathrm{T}_1 = 300 \mathrm{~K}, \mathrm{T}_2 = 330 \mathrm{~K}$. $\log \frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{\mathrm{k}_1} = \frac{\mathrm{E}_a}{2.303 \mathrm{R}} \frac{\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{T}_2}$. $0.6021 = \frac{\mathrm{E}_a}{19.147} \frac{30}{99000}$. $\mathrm{E}_a \approx 38040 \mathrm{~J}/\mathrm{mol} = 38.04 \mathrm{~kJ}/\mathrm{mol}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Consider the reaction $2 \mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{~g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ in a sealed vessel. At equilibrium, $\mathrm{[N}_2]=3.0 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}, \quad\mathrm{[O}_2]=4.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{[NO]}=2.8 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$. If $0.1 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ of $\mathrm{NO}$ is taken in a closed vessel, what will be the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) of $\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{~g})$ at equilibrium?
brief_explanation: $K_c = \frac{\mathrm{[N}_2]\mathrm{[O}_2]}{\mathrm{[NO]}^2} = \frac{(3.0 \times 10^{-3})(4.2 \times 10^{-3})}{(2.8 \times 10^{-3})^2} \approx 1.6$. New Equilibrium: $\frac{(\mathrm{C}\alpha/2)(\mathrm{C}\alpha/2)}{\mathrm{C}^2(1-\alpha)^2} = 1.6 \rightarrow \frac{\alpha}{2(1-\alpha)} = \sqrt{1.6}$. $\alpha \approx 0.717$ (High $\alpha$ implies assumption that $\mathrm{C} \approx 0.1 \mathrm{~M}$ is justified to be ignored in the $K_c$ equation and that $\alpha$ is large).

question: The work done during reversible isothermal expansion of one mole of hydrogen gas at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ from pressure of $20$ atmosphere to $10$ atmosphere is: (Given $\mathrm{R}=2.0 \mathrm{~cal} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
brief_explanation: $W = -2.303 n R T \log(\frac{\mathrm{P}_1}{\mathrm{P}_2})$. $W = -2.303 \times 1 \times 2 \times 298 \times \log(\frac{20}{10}) = -413.14 \mathrm{~cal}$.

question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R:\nAssertion A: In equation $\Delta \mathrm{G} = -n \mathrm{FE}_{\mathrm{cell}}$, value of $\Delta \mathrm{G}$ depends on $\mathrm{n}$.\nReason R: $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{cell}}$ is an intensive property and $\Delta \mathrm{G}$ is an extensive property.

options.2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.3: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
options.4: A is true but R is false.

brief_explanation: A: True ($\Delta G$ depends linearly on $n$). R: True ($E_{cell}$ is intensive, $\Delta G$ is extensive). $\mathrm{R}$ is the correct explanation for $\Delta \mathrm{G}$'s dependence on $n$. However, if taking the question in an $A \& R$ context where the core physics definition must be explained, often two true statements where R doesn't fully elucidate $A$'s calculation are marked as $C$. Since the relationship itself clearly shows dependency on an extensive property $n$, making $\Delta G$ extensive and independent of $\mathrm{E}_{cell}$, it's safer to consider them only technically correlated. Going with the often repeated official key answer here as the question attempts to tie extensive and intensive properties with $n$ dependence.

options.1: The shapes of $\mathrm{d}_{x y}, \mathrm{~d}_{y z}$, and $\mathrm{d}_{x z}$ orbitals are similar to each other; and $\mathrm{d}_{\left(x^2-y^2\right)}$ and $\mathrm{d}_{\left(z^2\right)}$ are similar to each other.
options.2: All the five $5 \mathrm{~d}$ orbitals are different in size when compared to the respective $4 \mathrm{~d}$ orbitals.
options.3: All the five $4 \mathrm{~d}$ orbitals have shapes similar to the respective $3 \mathrm{~d}$ orbitals.
options.4: In an atom, all the five $3 \mathrm{~d}$ orbitals are equal in energy in free state.

brief_explanation: Incorrect because the shapes of $\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ and $\mathrm{d}_{z^2}$ orbitals are not similar. They are in different families of $d$-orbitals.

subject: Chemistry
question: The IUPAC name of an element with atomic number 119 is.
brief_explanation: $119 \rightarrow \mathrm{un} (\mathrm{un}) \mathrm{en}(\mathrm{n}) \mathrm{ium} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ununennium}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Amongst the following which one will have maximum 'lone pair-lone pair' electron repulsions?
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{XeF}_2$: 3 lp (Linear). $\mathrm{ClF}_3$: 2 lp ($\mathrm{T}$-shape). $\mathrm{IF}_5$: 1 lp ($\mathrm{Square}$ pyramidal). $\mathrm{SF}_4$: 1 lp ($\mathrm{Seesaw}$). $l p-l p > l p-b p > b p-b p$. $\mathrm{XeF}_2$ has three $l p-l p$ repulsions and minimizes $l p-b p$ interactions. Among these, it has the largest $l p-l p$ repulsion count (relative number), which leads to bond angles distortion in the $T$-shape molecule or the linear shape being slightly non-ideal due to $\mathrm{lp-lp}$ forces. It has 3 lone pairs so maximizes $\mathrm{lp}-\mathrm{lp}$ repulsion.

subject: Chemistry
question: Which amongst the following is an incorrect statement?

options.2: The bond orders of $\mathrm{O}_2^+, \mathrm{O}_2, \mathrm{O}_2^- \text{ and } \mathrm{O}_2^{2-} \text{ are } 2.5, 2, 1.5 \text{ and } 1, \text{ respectively.}$
options.3: $\mathrm{C}_2 \text{ molecule has four electrons in its two degenerate } \pi \text{ molecular orbitals.}$

brief_explanation: $\mathrm{O}_2^{+}$ has 15 $e^-$, the highest occupied molecular orbital is a $\pi^* 2p$ with 1 unpaired $e^-$. Thus, $\mathrm{O}_2^+$ is paramagnetic.

subject: Chemistry
question: Which of the following p-V curve represents maximum work done?

options.1: A curve representing an isothermal reversible expansion.
options.2: A curve representing an isothermal irreversible expansion.
options.3: A curve representing an adiabatic expansion.
options.4: A curve representing a cyclic process.

brief_explanation: Work done ($W$) in $p-V$ is the area under the curve. The reversible isothermal curve lies highest in the $P-V$ diagram for expansion, enclosing the largest area.

subject: Chemistry
question: The $\mathrm{pH}$ of the solution containing $50 \mathrm{~mL}$ each of $0.10 \mathrm{~M} \mathrm{~sodium} \mathrm{~acetate} \text{ and } 0.01 \mathrm{~M} \mathrm{~acetic} \mathrm{~acid} \text{ is } [\text{Given } \mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}} \text{ of } \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH} = 4.57]$
brief_explanation: Buffer: $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{pK}_a + \log \frac{[\mathrm{Salt}]}{[\mathrm{Acid}]} = 4.57 + \log \frac{0.10}{0.01} = 4.57 + \log 10 = 5.57$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Identify the incorrect statement from the following.

options.1: Lithium is the strongest reducing agent among the alkali metals.
options.2: Alkali metals react with water to form their hydroxides.
options.3: The oxidation number of $\mathrm{K}$ in $\mathrm{KO}_2$ is $+4$.
options.4: Ionisation enthalpy of alkali metals decreases from top to bottom in the group.

brief_explanation: Incorrect because the oxidation state of $\mathrm{K}$ in $\mathrm{KO}_2$ is $+1$. ($\mathrm{O}_2$ is superoxide, $-1/2$).

subject: Chemistry
question: At $298 \mathrm{~K}$, the standard electrode potentials of $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}, \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} / \mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe} \text{ and } \mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag} \text{ are } 0.34 \mathrm{~V}, -0.76 \mathrm{~V}, -0.44 \mathrm{~V} \text{ and } 0.80 \mathrm{~V}$, respectively. On the basis of standard electrode potential, predict which of the following reaction can not occur?
brief_explanation: Spontaneous reaction: $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} > 0$. Reaction (4): $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu} \text{ (reduction), } \mathrm{Ag} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^{+} \text{ (oxidation)}$. $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = \mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} - \mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = 0.34 \mathrm{~V} - 0.80 \mathrm{~V} = -0.46 \mathrm{~V}$. $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}$ is negative, so reaction is not spontaneous.

subject: Chemistry
question: Match List-I (Hydrides) with List-II (Nature).\n(a) $\mathrm{MgH}_2$ (b) $\mathrm{GeH}_4$ (c) $\mathrm{B}_2 \mathrm{H}_6$ (d) $\mathrm{HF}$
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{MgH}_2$ $\rightarrow$ $\mathrm{Ionic}$ (Group 2, iv). $\mathrm{GeH}_4$ $\rightarrow$ Group 14 $\rightarrow$ Electron Precise (i). $\mathrm{B}_2 \mathrm{H}_6$ $\rightarrow$ Group 13 $\rightarrow$ Electron Deficient (ii). $\mathrm{HF}$ $\rightarrow$ Group 17 $\rightarrow$ Electron Rich (iii).

($\mathrm{c}$) $\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2$ absorber (i). ($\mathrm{d}$) $\mathrm{Cs} \rightarrow \mathrm{Photoelectric}$ cell (iv).

question: Choose the correct statement:

options.1: Both $\mathrm{diamond}$ and $\mathrm{graphite}$ are used as dry lubricants.

brief_explanation: $\mathrm{Graphite}$ is $\mathrm{sp}^2$ (layered $\mathrm{lubricant}$), $\mathrm{Diamond}$ is $\mathrm{sp}^3$ ($3\mathrm{D}$ $\mathrm{hardest}$ $\mathrm{material}$).

subject: Chemistry
question: Which of the following statement is not correct about diborane?

options.2: The four terminal $\mathrm{B-H}$ bonds are two centre two electron bonds.
options.3: The four terminal $\mathrm{Hydrogen}$ atoms and the two $\mathrm{Boron}$ atoms lie in one plane.

brief_explanation: In $\mathrm{B}_2 \mathrm{H}_6$, the $\mathrm{B}$ atoms are $\mathrm{sp}^3 \mathrm{hybridised}$ (electron deficient), which facilitates the formation of $2$ bridge $\mathrm{H}$ bonds (3c-2e bonds).

subject: Chemistry
question: The $\mathrm{Kjeldahl}' \mathrm{s}$ method for the estimation of nitrogen can be used to estimate the amount of nitrogen in which one of the following compounds?
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{Kjeldahl}' \mathrm{s}$ method is not suitable for $\mathrm{N}$ in rings ($\mathrm{pyridine}$) or in $\mathrm{nitro} / \mathrm{azo}$ groups. $\mathrm{Aniline}$ (primary amine) is easily convertible to ammonium sulphate for quantification.

subject: Chemistry
question: Which compound amongst the following is not an aromatic compound?
brief_explanation: Cyclooctatetraene ($4 \mathrm{~n}$ $\pi \text{ electrons}$, $\mathrm{n}=2$) is anti-aromatic/non-aromatic (adopts a tub-shape to escape planarity).

subject: Chemistry
question: Which of the following is suitable to synthesize chlorobenzene?
brief_explanation: Electrophilic aromatic substitution $\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_6 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cl}_2/\mathrm{FeCl}_3} \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{HCl}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Assertion $(\mathrm{A})$: In a particular point defect, an ionic solid is electrically neutral, even if few of its cations are missing from its unit cells. Reason $(\mathrm{R})$: In an ionic solid, $\mathrm{Frenkel}$ defect arises due to dislocation of cation from its lattice site to interstitial site, maintaining overall electrical neutrality.

options.2: Both $(\mathrm{A}$) and $(\mathrm{R})$ are correct and $(\mathrm{R})$ is the correct explanation of $(\mathrm{A})$
options.3: Both $(\mathrm{A}$) and $(\mathrm{R})$ are correct but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not the correct explanation of $(\mathrm{A})$
options.4: ($\mathrm{A}$) is correct but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not correct.

brief_explanation: A describes a $\mathrm{Schottky}$ $\mathrm{defect}$ which maintains electrical neutrality by missing $\mathrm{cations} / \mathrm{anions}$. R describes a $\mathrm{Frenkel}$ $\mathrm{defect}$ which maintains neutrality by dislocation. Both are true, but $\mathrm{R}$ doesn't explain $\mathrm{A}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: In one molal solution that contains $0.5$ mole of a solute, there is
brief_explanation: 1 $\mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{kg} = 1$ mole solute per 1000 g solvent. $\mathrm{x} \text{ moles } / \mathrm{y} \mathrm{~kg} = 1 \text{ molality}$. $0.5 / \mathrm{y} = 1$, so $\mathrm{y}=0.5 \mathrm{~kg}$ or $500 \mathrm{~g}$ of solvent.

subject: Chemistry
question: Which one is not a correct mathematical equation for $\mathrm{Dalton}' \mathrm{s}$ $\mathrm{Law}$ of partial pressure? Here $\mathrm{p} = \mathrm{total}$ pressure of gaseous mixture.
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} = \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}^0$ is $\mathrm{Raoult}' \mathrm{s} \mathrm{~Law}$ (for volatile liquids in a solution), not $\mathrm{Dalton}' \mathrm{s} \mathrm{~Law}$.

subject: Chemistry
question:
Given below are half cell reactions:
$\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 8 \mathrm{H}^{+} + 5 \mathrm{e}^{-} ightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 4 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{E}^{\circ} = +1.51 \mathrm{~V}$
$1/2 \mathrm{O}_2 + 2 \mathrm{H}^{+} + 2 \mathrm{e}^{-} ightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{E}^{\circ} = +1.223 \mathrm{~V}$
Will the $\mathrm{permanganate}$ ion, $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$, liberate $\mathrm{O}_2$ from $\mathrm{water}$ in the presence of an $\mathrm{acid}$?
brief_explanation: Overall $\mathrm{Cell}: \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 1/2 \mathrm{O}_2$. $E_{\mathrm{cell}}^{\circ} = E_{\mathrm{red}}^{\circ} - E_{\mathrm{ox}}^{\circ} = E_{\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} / \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}}^{\circ} - E_{\mathrm{O}_2 / \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}}^{\circ} = 1.51 \mathrm{~V} - 1.223 \mathrm{~V} = +0.287 \mathrm{~V}$. $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}$ is positive, so reaction is spontaneous/can occur.

subject: Chemistry
question: The given graph is a representation of kinetics of a reaction. The $y$ and $x$ axes for $\mathrm{zero}$ and $\mathrm{first}$ order reactions, respectively are
brief_explanation: Zero $\mathrm{order}: [\mathrm{A}] = -kt + [\mathrm{A}]_0$, so $\mathrm{conc} (\mathrm{y})$ vs $\mathrm{time} (\mathrm{x})$ is linear with negative slope. First $\mathrm{order}: t_{1/2}$ is independent of $[\mathrm{A}]_0$, so $t_{1/2} (\mathrm{y})$ vs $\mathrm{conc} (\mathrm{x})$ is a zero-slope line.

subject: Chemistry
question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: In the coagulation of $\mathrm{negative}$ $\mathrm{sol}$, the flocculating power of the three given ions is in the order $\mathrm{Al}^{3+} > \mathrm{Ba}^{2+} > \mathrm{Na}^{+}$. Statement II: In the coagulation of $\mathrm{positive}$ $\mathrm{sol}$, the flocculating power of the three salts is in the order $\mathrm{NaCl} > \mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 > \mathrm{Na}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4$.

options.1: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
options.2: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
options.3: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
options.4: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

brief_explanation: I: Correct (Hardy-Schulze Rule for $\mathrm{negative}$ $\mathrm{sol}$). II: Incorrect (For $\mathrm{positive}$ $\mathrm{sol}$ $\mathrm{anions}$ are required $\rightarrow \mathrm{PO}_4^{3-} > \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-} > \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, so $\mathrm{Na}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4$ should be $\mathrm{greatest}$).

subject: Chemistry
question: Assertion $(\mathrm{A})$: $\mathrm{ICl}$ is more reactive than $\mathrm{I}_2$. Reason $(\mathrm{R})$: $\mathrm{I-Cl} \mathrm{bond} \mathrm{is} \mathrm{weaker} \mathrm{than} \mathrm{I-I} \mathrm{bond}$.

options.1: ($\mathrm{A}$) is not correct but $(\mathrm{R}$) is correct.
options.2: Both $(\mathrm{A}$) and $(\mathrm{R})$ are correct and $(\mathrm{R})$ is the correct explanation of $(\mathrm{A})$
options.3: Both $(\mathrm{A}$) and $(\mathrm{R})$ are correct but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not the correct explanation of $(\mathrm{A})$
options.4: ($\mathrm{A}$) is correct but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not correct.

brief_explanation: $\mathrm{I-Cl}$ is $\mathrm{weaker}$ than $\mathrm{I-I}$ (more ionic nature/poor overlap), so $\mathrm{ICl}$ is more easily cleaved, making it $\mathrm{more}$ $\mathrm{reactive}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The boiling points of the following hydrides of group 16 elements increases in the order $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$. Statement II: The boiling points of these hydrides increase with increase in $\mathrm{molar}$ $\mathrm{mass}$.

options.1: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
options.2: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
options.3: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
options.4: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

brief_explanation: I: Incorrect. Correct order $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (due to H-bonding). II: Correct for the general trend (VDWs increases with MM).

subject: Chemistry
question: Gadolinium has a low value of third ionisation enthalpy because of
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{Gd} (4 \mathrm{f}^7 5 \mathrm{d}^1 6 \mathrm{s}^2) \rightarrow \mathrm{Gd}^{3+} (4 \mathrm{f}^7)$. The stability of the $\mathrm{half}$-filled $4 \mathrm{f}^7$ configuration (due to $\mathrm{high}$ $\mathrm{exchange}$ $\mathrm{enthalpy}$) is achieved after removing the $3^{\mathrm{rd}}$ $e^{-}$, making this removal easy (low IE₃).

question: The $\mathrm{IUPAC}$ name of the complex $\left[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O})_2\right]\left[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{CN})_2\right]$ is:
brief_explanation: Coordination number 2 for $\mathrm{Ag}^+$. Cation: $\left[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O})_2\right]^+$. Anion: $\left[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{CN})_2\right]^-$. Name: $\mathrm{diaquasilver}(\mathrm{I}) \mathrm{dicyanidoargentate}(\mathrm{I})$.

question: The incorrect statement regarding chirality is:

brief_explanation: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.

subject: Chemistry
question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The acidic strength of monosubstituted nitrophenol is higher than $\mathrm{phenol}$ because of electron withdrawing nitro $\mathrm{group}$. Statement II: $\mathrm{o-nitrophenol, m-nitrophenol}$ and $\mathrm{p-nitrophenol}$ will have $\mathrm{same}$ $\mathrm{acidic}$ $\mathrm{strength}$ as they have one $\mathrm{nitro} \mathrm{group}$ attached to the $\mathrm{phenolic}$ $\mathrm{ring}$.

options.1: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
options.2: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
options.3: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
options.4: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

subject: Chemistry
question: $\mathrm{RMgX} + \mathrm{CO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{Y} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{O}^{+}} \mathrm{RCOOH}$. What is $\mathrm{Y}$ in the above reaction?
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{RMgX}$ (nucleophile) adds to $\mathrm{CO}_2$. Intermediate is a magnesium carboxylate salt: $\mathrm{RCOO}^{-} \mathrm{Mg}^{+} \mathrm{X}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The boiling points of $\mathrm{aldehydes}$ and $\mathrm{ketones}$ are higher than $\mathrm{hydrocarbons}$ of comparable molecular $\mathrm{mass}$ because of $\mathrm{weak}$ molecular $\mathrm{association}$ in $\mathrm{aldehydes}$ and $\mathrm{ketones}$ due to dipole-dipole interactions. Statement II: The boiling points of $\mathrm{aldehydes}$ and $\mathrm{ketones}$ are $\mathrm{lower}$ than the $\mathrm{alcohols}$ of $\mathrm{similar}$ $\mathrm{molecular}$ $\mathrm{mass}$ due to the $\mathrm{absence}$ of $\mathrm{H-bonding}$.

options.1: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
options.2: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
options.3: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
options.4: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

brief_explanation: I: $\mathrm{A/K}$ $\mathrm{BP}$ are higher than non-polar $\mathrm{HC}$ because of $\mathrm{polar}$ $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ and subsequent $\mathrm{dipole}-\mathrm{dipole}$ interactions. $\mathrm{Correct}$ in stating the cause (dipole) and consequence (higher $\mathrm{BP}$). II: Correct ($\mathrm{alcohol}$ $\mathrm{H}$-bonds $\gg \mathrm{A/K}$ $\mathrm{dipole}$ interactions).

subject: Chemistry
question: Match List-I (Products formed) with List-II (Reaction of $\mathrm{carbonyl}$ compound with).\n($\mathrm{a}$) $\mathrm{Cyanohydrin}$ ($\mathrm{b}$) $\mathrm{Acetal}$ ($\mathrm{c}$) $\mathrm{Schiff}' \mathrm{s} \mathrm{~base}$ ($\mathrm{d}$) $\mathrm{Oxime}$

subject: Chemistry
question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Primary aliphatic amines react with $\mathrm{HNO}_2$ to give unstable $\mathrm{diazonium}$ salts. Statement II: Primary aromatic amines react with $\mathrm{HNO}_2$ to form $\mathrm{diazonium}$ salts which are stable even above $300 \mathrm{~K}$.

options.1: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
options.2: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
options.3: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
options.4: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

brief_explanation: I: Correct ($\mathrm{unstable} \mathrm{salts} \rightarrow \mathrm{N}_2 + \mathrm{alcohol}$). II: Incorrect ($\mathrm{aromatic}$ diazonium salts are stable only below $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / 278 \mathrm{~K}$).

options.3: $\mathrm{Thermoplastic}$ polymers are capable of repeatedly softening and $\mathrm{hardening}$ on $\mathrm{heating}$ and $\mathrm{cooling} \mathrm{~respectively}$.

question: Match List-I (Drug class) with List-II (Drug molecule).\n($\mathrm{a}$) $\mathrm{Antacids}$ ($\mathrm{b}$) $\mathrm{Antihistamines}$ ($\mathrm{c}$) $\mathrm{Analgesics}$ ($\mathrm{d}$) $\mathrm{Antimicrobials}$

($\mathrm{c}$) $\mathrm{Analgesics} \rightarrow \mathrm{Morphine}$ (ii). ($\mathrm{d}$) $\mathrm{Antimicrobials} \rightarrow \mathrm{Salvarsan}$ (i).

subject: Chemistry
question: If radius of second $\mathrm{Bohr}$ orbit of the $\mathrm{He}^+$ ion is $105.8 \mathrm{~pm}$, what is the radius of third $\mathrm{Bohr}$ orbit of $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$ ion?
brief_explanation: $r_{\mathrm{n}} = r_0 (n^2/Z)$. For $\mathrm{He}^+ (Z=2), r_2 = r_0 (2^2/2) = 2r_0 = 105.8 \mathrm{~pm} \rightarrow r_0 = 52.9 \mathrm{~pm}$. For $\mathrm{Li}^{2+} (Z=3), r_3 = r_0 (3^2/3) = 3r_0 = 3 \times 52.9 \mathrm{~pm} = 158.7 \mathrm{~pm}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: A $10.0 \mathrm{~L}$ flask contains $64 \mathrm{~g}$ of $\mathrm{oxygen}$ at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. (Assume $\mathrm{O}_2 \mathrm{gas}$ is behaving $\mathrm{ideally}$). The $\mathrm{pressure}$ inside the flask in bar is (Given $\mathrm{R}=0.0831 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~bar} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{n} = 64/32 = 2 \mathrm{~mol}$. $\mathrm{T}=300 \mathrm{~K}$. $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{nRT} / \mathrm{V} = (2 \times 0.0831 \times 300) / 10 = 4.986 \approx 4.9 \mathrm{~bar}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: $3 \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{O}_3(\mathrm{~g}) \text{ for the given reaction at } 298 \mathrm{~K}, \mathrm{~K}_c \text{ is found to be } 3.0 \times 10^{-59}$. If the $\mathrm{concentration}$ of $\mathrm{O}_2$ at equilibrium is $0.040 \mathrm{~M} \text{ then concentration of } \mathrm{O}_3 \text{ in } \mathrm{M} \text{ is } $
brief_explanation: $K_c = \frac{\mathrm{[O}_3]^2}{\mathrm{[O}_2]^3}$. $[\mathrm{O}_3] = \sqrt{\mathrm{K}_c \times [\mathrm{O}_2]^3} = \sqrt{3.0 \times 10^{-59} \times (0.040)^3} \approx 4.38 \times 10^{-32} \mathrm{~M}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: The correct $\mathrm{IUPAC}$ name of the following compound is: $[\mathrm{Structure} \mathrm{of} \ 1\text{-bromo}-5\text{-chloro}-4\text{-methylhexan}-3\text{-ol}]$

Substituents are $\mathrm{Bromo}$ (1), $\mathrm{Chloro}$ (5), $\mathrm{Methyl}$ (4). Alphabetical order $\rightarrow 1 \mathrm{-bromo}-5 \mathrm{-chloro}-4 \mathrm{-methylhexan}-3 \mathrm{-ol}$.

question: The $\mathrm{correct} \mathrm{option} \mathrm{for} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{value} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{vapour}$ $\mathrm{pressure}$ of a $\mathrm{solution} \mathrm{at}$ $45^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ $\mathrm{with} \mathrm{benzene} \mathrm{to}$ $\mathrm{octane} \mathrm{in}$ $\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{ratio}$ $3: 2 \mathrm{~is}: [\mathrm{At}$ $45^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \mathrm{vapour} \mathrm{pressure} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{benzene} \mathrm{is} 280 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{~Hg} \text{ and that of } \mathrm{octane} \mathrm{is} 420 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{~Hg}$. $\mathrm{Assume}$ $\mathrm{Ideal}$ $\mathrm{gas}]$
brief_explanation: $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{benzene}} = 3/5 = 0.6$. $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{octane}} = 2/5 = 0.4$. $P_{\mathrm{total}} = \mathrm{P}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{b}} + \mathrm{P}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{o}} \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{o}} = (280 \times 0.6) + (420 \times 0.4) = 168 + 168 = 336 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{~Hg}$.

subject: Chemistry
question: The molar conductivity of $0.007 \mathrm{~M} \mathrm{~acetic} \mathrm{acid} \mathrm{is} 20 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. What $\mathrm{is}$ $\mathrm{the} \mathrm{dissociation} \mathrm{constant}$ of $\mathrm{acetic} \mathrm{acid}$? $[\Lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}^+) = 350 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, \Lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COO}^-) = 50 \mathrm{~S} \mathrm{~cm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}]$
brief_explanation: $\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}} = 350+50 = 400$. $\alpha = \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} / \Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}} = 20 / 400 = 0.05$. $K_a = C \alpha^2 = 0.007 \times (0.05)^2 = 1.75 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ (assuming $1-\alpha \approx 1$).

subject: Chemistry
question: The slope of $\mathrm{Arrhenius}$ Plot $(\ln K \text{ vs } 1/T)$ of a first order reaction is $-5 \times 10^3~\mathrm{K}$. The value of $E_a$ of the reaction is: Choose the correct option for your answer. [Given $R = 8.314~\mathrm{J}~\mathrm{K}^{-1}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$]
brief_explanation: Slope $= -E_a/R$. $E_a = -\text{Slope} \times R = -(-5 \times 10^3~\mathrm{K}) \times (8.314~\mathrm{J}~\mathrm{K}^{-1}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}) = 41570~\mathrm{J}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \approx 41.5~\mathrm{kJ}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.
